lesson.title: When One Atom Simply Takes the Electron
lesson.summary: Ionic bonds form when a large electronegativity difference drives one atom to fully transfer a valence electron to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
lesson.body:
An ionic bond is the most extreme outcome that chemical bonds can produce: rather than sharing a pair of valence electrons, one atom gives an electron up entirely and the other takes it, and the resulting bond is simply the electrostatic attraction between the two oppositely charged ions that are created. This only happens between atoms with a large electronegativity difference, typically a metal on the low end of the electronegativity scale paired with a nonmetal on the high end, because the electronegativity gap is what makes an even split of the shared electrons impossible. A rough rule of thumb places the ionic threshold around an electronegativity difference of 1.7 or greater, though this line is a convenient approximation rather than a strict boundary.

Sodium chloride is the textbook case, and walking through it makes the energy bookkeeping clear. Sodium's first ionization energy is 496 kilojoules per mole, the energy required to strip its lone valence electron away and form Na+. Chlorine's electron affinity is negative 349 kilojoules per mole, the energy released when it accepts that electron and becomes Cl-. Simply adding those two steps together, plus 496 and minus 349, gives a net cost of positive 147 kilojoules per mole just to transfer the electron between two isolated gas phase atoms, meaning electron transfer alone is actually unfavorable. What makes sodium chloride form spontaneously is that the resulting ions do not stay as isolated gas phase particles, they come together and release a large amount of additional energy as they arrange into a crystal lattice, more than enough to cover that 147 kilojoule per mole deficit. This lattice energy release is covered in detail later, but the key point here is that electron transfer by itself is only the first, energetically uphill step of ionic bond formation.

The electronegativity connection also explains which elements pair up to form ionic bonds in the first place. Elements with low ionization energies, mostly the metals on the left side of the periodic table, correspond to low electronegativity values, since both properties reflect how weakly an atom holds its own valence electrons. Elements with strongly negative electron affinities, mostly the nonmetals on the right side, correspond to high electronegativity values, since both reflect how strongly an atom attracts additional electrons. Putting a low electronegativity metal next to a high electronegativity nonmetal creates exactly the large electronegativity gap that makes full electron transfer more favorable than equal sharing.

Once formed, the resulting ions typically reach a stable, noble gas like electron configuration, part of why the transfer happens at the specific number of electrons that it does. Sodium loses one electron to go from 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 to 1s2 2s2 2p6, matching neon's configuration, while chlorine gains one electron to go from a configuration one electron short of argon to argon's full configuration exactly. This is not a coincidence: elements tend to transfer the number of electrons that gets them to a filled valence shell and stop there, which is also why successive ionization energy data showed such a sharp jump right after an element's valence electrons were used up. The unlike charges left behind, Na+ and Cl-, then attract each other according to Coulomb's law, and that electrostatic attraction, multiplied across billions of ion pairs arranged in an orderly repeating pattern, is what actually holds an ionic solid together.
